name: Gluteus maximus
func: The biggest muscle in the body, forming the buttock. It powerfully straightens the hip for climbing, running and standing up, and helps keep the trunk upright.

levels.kid:
The **gluteus maximus** is the **biggest muscle in your whole body**! It is the big muscle that makes up your bottom, the part you sit on.

It is super strong because it has a big job. It pulls your leg **backward** and helps you **stand up** from a chair, **climb stairs**, jump and run fast. It also keeps you standing tall instead of tipping forward.

When you sit, it gets out of the way so you sit on your hip bones and a cushion of fat. Animals that walk on four legs have much smaller ones than people do.
levels.hs:
The **gluteus maximus** is the largest and most superficial of the **gluteal muscles** (buttock muscles). It lies just under the skin and fat of the buttock, covering the smaller **gluteus medius** and **gluteus minimus**, and the deep hip rotators such as **piriformis**.

It starts from the back of the **ilium** (behind the posterior gluteal line), the back of the **sacrum** and **coccyx**, and the **sacrotuberous ligament**. Its thick fibres run down and outward. Most of the muscle (the upper part and the superficial lower part) inserts into the **iliotibial tract (IT band)**, a strong band of fascia running down the outside of the thigh to the tibia. The deeper lower fibres insert on the **gluteal tuberosity** of the femur.

Its main action is **extending the hip** (pulling the thigh backward, or straightening the body when the thigh is fixed). It also **laterally rotates** the thigh. Through the IT band, it helps stabilise the extended knee.

It is supplied by the **inferior gluteal nerve** (L5–S2). In ordinary walking on flat ground it is only mildly active; it works hardest in **climbing stairs, running, jumping and rising from sitting**. The **sciatic nerve** runs deep to it, which is why injections into the buttock are given only in the upper outer part.
levels.college:
**Attachments:** origin from the posterior gluteal surface of the ilium behind the posterior gluteal line, the iliac crest, the dorsal surfaces of the sacrum and coccyx, the erector spinae aponeurosis and the sacrotuberous ligament. Insertion: about three-quarters into the **iliotibial tract** and the rest into the **gluteal tuberosity**.

**Nerve and vessels:** the **inferior gluteal nerve (L5, S1, S2)** and **inferior gluteal artery** exit the pelvis through the **greater sciatic foramen below piriformis**, together with the sciatic nerve and the posterior femoral cutaneous nerve. The **superior gluteal artery** also supplies its upper part.

**Deep relations:** under the gluteus maximus lie gluteus medius, piriformis, the superior and inferior gemelli with obturator internus between them, and quadratus femoris, from above down. The **sciatic nerve** emerges below piriformis and runs down over the short lateral rotators, roughly midway between the **ischial tuberosity** and the **greater trochanter**. Several **bursae** separate the muscle from the greater trochanter and the ischial tuberosity.

**Function:** it is a powerful hip extensor, mainly when force is high or the hip is flexed. It also **laterally rotates** the hip; its upper fibres help abduct and its lower fibres help adduct. It controls forward lean of the trunk on the hip when bending and lifting, and decelerates hip flexion at heel strike.

**Safe injection site:** the **upper outer quadrant** of the buttock (or more precisely the ventrogluteal site over gluteus medius) avoids the sciatic nerve and the inferior gluteal neurovascular bundle.
levels.phd:
The gluteus maximus is a hallmark of human evolution. In chimpanzees, the homologous muscle is relatively small and arises mostly from the ischium (the "gluteus maximus ischiofemoralis"), acting more as a hip extensor and abductor during climbing. In humans, the cranial portion has expanded greatly, originating from the ilium and sacrum.

**Bramble and Lieberman** proposed that this expansion is an adaptation for **endurance running**. EMG studies show the human gluteus maximus is relatively quiet during walking but strongly active during running, where it stabilises the trunk against forward pitching at each foot strike and decelerates the swinging leg. This supports the view that bipedal running, not just walking, shaped human hip anatomy, although other researchers emphasise climbing, throwing or tool use.

Its architecture favours force: a large **physiological cross-sectional area**, long fascicles and a long moment arm for hip extension, especially when the hip is flexed. Its fibres connect to the **thoracolumbar fascia** and, via the sacrotuberous ligament, to the opposite latissimus dorsi, forming the **posterior oblique sling** that transfers load across the **sacroiliac joint** during gait (the concept of **force closure**).

The insertion into the IT band makes the gluteus maximus and **tensor fasciae latae** together a "deltoid of the hip". The IT band stores and returns elastic energy during running, a mechanism studied in biomechanical models.

Its motor neurons in the L5–S2 ventral horn receive strong descending vestibulospinal and reticulospinal input, consistent with its role in upright posture.
levels.expert:
**Exam:** test hip extension prone with the knee flexed (to reduce hamstring contribution) against resistance. Observe gait: weakness causes a **gluteus maximus (backward-lurching) gait**, where the patient throws the trunk backward at heel strike to keep the hip extended. This differs from the **Trendelenburg gait** of gluteus medius weakness (pelvis drops on the opposite side in single-leg stance).

**Inferior gluteal nerve injury** is uncommon: posterior approaches to the hip, intramuscular injections in the wrong spot, or pelvic fractures. Patients struggle to climb stairs and rise from a chair.

**Sciatic nerve injury from buttock injections** remains a known complication worldwide, causing foot drop and pain; correct site selection prevents it.

**Piriformis syndrome**: buttock pain radiating down the leg, attributed to irritation of the sciatic nerve by piriformis deep to gluteus maximus; it is a diagnosis of exclusion, and lumbar radiculopathy must be ruled out with exam and MRI.

**Bursitis**: ischial bursitis from prolonged sitting on hard surfaces; trochanteric pain syndrome (mostly gluteus medius/minimus tendinopathy). **Hamstring and gluteal injuries** in sprinters are distinguished by MRI.

**Pressure ulcers** over the sacrum and ischial tuberosities develop in immobile patients; the gluteus maximus is often rotated or advanced as a **musculocutaneous flap** to close these wounds.

In **posterior hip surgery** (hip replacement, acetabular fracture fixation), the gluteus maximus is split along its fibres (the Kocher–Langenbeck approach), and the sciatic nerve is protected beneath. In low lumbar or sacral cord lesions, hip flexors (L2–L3) may work while the hip extensors (L5–S2) are weak.

keyPoints: Largest muscle in the body; most superficial gluteal muscle
Inserts mainly into the iliotibial tract and gluteal tuberosity
Powerful hip extensor and lateral rotator
Sciatic nerve lies deep to it → inject only in the upper outer area

test.q: What is the main action of gluteus maximus?
test.explain: It extends the hip powerfully, e.g. climbing stairs and standing up.

test.q: Which nerve supplies the gluteus maximus? (two words)
test.explain: The superior gluteal nerve supplies gluteus medius and minimus instead.

test.q: Most of gluteus maximus inserts into which structure?
test.explain: About three-quarters inserts into the IT tract; the rest into the gluteal tuberosity.

test.q: Weak gluteus maximus classically causes which gait?
test.explain: The trunk is thrown back at heel strike to keep the hip extended.

test.q: Which large nerve runs deep to gluteus maximus?
test.explain: Injections in the upper outer buttock avoid it.
